p:
We need some work really done. Being on the radar is one thing, but getting it done is the next thing. So, we really need, because we constantly get complaints from constituents on this issue. And I don't know if it's a budgetary issue, a lack of manpower, but these trees are causing damage to residents' properties. And we're constantly hearing about the, you know,

that the complaints are being made, but nothing's being done. So, I want to move on to this question. Given the unresolved issues, Parks recently proceeded with plans to plant an additional tree adjacent to this particular property before the existing problem was dealt with. So, I want to understand how's that done. If a resident's complaining that a tree is doing damage to their property, and then the next couple of days they wake up and there's another tree planted, what's the priority here?

Sure. The priority is most definitely to, of course, serve New Yorkers. So, very much so the priorities, but the kind of devils in the details, right? So, we want to plant in every plantable area possible in our city, and I'm frankly very happy to hear that that means that we're hitting at least one of your streets on the higher list within that nine-year cycle that we're looking at. So, I'm happy to hear that some of your constituents are getting to see that early on. So, one, we are planting, but two, of course, we are also pruning the existing trees, and we mentioned before in our testimony that ultimately our

prioritization has to go down from like the most extreme loss of life sort of concerns around dangerous situations, and then we work our way down. It sounds like in this situation, although I'm happy to look into it further personally, is that it sounds like we're in procurement to get that tree pruning contract done, which is a good sign. That means that it's coming soon, but the folks who are doing the tree pruning are not necessarily the folks who are doing the planting. We have different teams that are doing that, so that's why you would see some work being done on planting and some work being done on pruning and not necessarily at the same time. Again, I would say that that's a good thing. That means that we don't have just one team that's doing it all, that your constituents can see some work that's being done on their tree beds, on new plantings in the area, but that certainly does not mean that we are forgetting about the work that needs to get done on pruning. Like I said, we're happy to take it back. It always goes back to that prioritization of safety, and so we do have looked at that, and of course, those things, as Ben has said, that can change. This is living infrastructure. A snowstorm, a windstorm, things like

that can change the situation, so we're happy to take a second look.

Okay. Now when it comes to tree work permits and private hire options, when the Parks suggest that a residence may hire a private company to prune a City tree, is there any viable pathway for reimbursement?

I believe that that may have to be looked at with the Comptroller's office, depending on the exact situation. I'm looking to our Assistant Commissioner, Ben Osborne, to share with us if that's correct. Just want to make sure I'm correct with that pathway.

That is my understanding. If there's an expense incurred to a property owner due to damage from a City tree to their property, the Comptroller would be the best place to address those types of questions.
Okay. And the last question, and I guess I'll come back in the second round if --
I just don't want to make everybody jealous, you know?
Oh, sorry. My last question, and I'll come back in the second round. Is that okay, Chair? Does the Parks maintain a list of pre-approved vendors or certified arborists for residents to use?

We do not recommend private contractors. You know, there's the potential for a conflict of interest there. However, we do recommend that people look at the qualifications of a contractor they may hire, and the International Society of Arboriculture provides the internationally recognized credential for that type of work.
Thank you, Chair, for your indulgence.

Sorry. If I could just really quickly interject and just clarify that a tree work permit is completely free of charge, right? So, the advice and the consultation that's provided by the agency, that expertise, you know, is available to the public and the folks they hire, you know, completely free of charge.

Thank you.

Before we move to the next Council Member, I just want to mention to my Colleagues, only because this seemingly was a highly anticipated hearing, we're going to institute the clock at this point, giving each Member five minutes, because we also want to hear from our advocates as well.

And excuse me, Chair, I just want to make mention, just because it's sitting in my mind, that your question about overtime for our recent storm, I just want to get back to you with final confirmation on when, what overtime was covered. We've been changing some of the systems around this, and so before, I think I said it was, I just want to triple confirm that with you, so we'll get back to you on exactly the overtime that was covered.
Thank you, thank you so much. Council Member Salaam.

Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Commissioner. Just a few questions here on health and inspections. DPR Tree Inspection program and Local Laws 20 and 59 of 2022 and 2025 have laid out

frameworks for prioritizing and maintaining the health of street trees. Can you elaborate on how these regulations are being implemented and monitored to ensure the health of trees in all five boroughs? And how does DPR ensure that these trees are inspected on time, and what improvements are being made to address the backlog or delays in pruning and maintenance?

First of all, I just want to say that it's my understanding that both of these local laws was done in partnership with our agency, so on behalf of our agency, thank you for continuing to work with us on thinking through ways that we can systematize and improve services to New Yorkers, particularly with our tree canopy. I will look to our Assistant Commissioner to give you an update on specifically how implementation of those local laws is going, but I will just say that our Block Pruning Program, which, again, looks to prune every single New York City street tree within a seven-year cycle, is really where we're looking at the gold standard. It is industry standard to do so, and so you can tell your constituents and you just understand that all of our

trees we're looking to prune on that seven-year cycle. But I'll look to our Assistant Commissioner to give you more specific updates on those two pieces of legislation.

Thank you for the question, and as far as Local Law 59 of 2025, so that specifically requires the Parks Department to incorporate a system for evaluating a building clearance prune request into our existing tree risk management protocol. So, we have developed the framework for those inspections, and we're putting the finishing touches on the technology that will allow us to perform those inspections and record the data. You know, this will provide a standard where there previously had not been a precise standard for evaluating these types of requests and working any work orders that result into our existing prioritization of work orders, and we expect to be fully compliant with the legislation when it goes into effect in May.

Thank you. The Neighborhood Tree Planting Program aims to address heat-vulnerable neighborhoods and increase canopy coverage to 30 percent. How does DPR track the

progress of this initiative, and how can the Council ensure all communities, especially those with lower tree density, are adequately served?

Thank you for your question. Our Neighborhood Tree Planting Program, the comprehensive approach that I referenced earlier in my testimony, was directly kind of grown out of the target for us to plant in heat-vulnerable neighborhoods and to complete those plantings of HVI 4 and 5 by the end of 2027. And so certainly we are tracking this very closely because we want to ensure that we reach that mark, that by the end of 2027, we have fully planted in HVI 4 and 5. But from there, as we've discussed, we've seen such success with this targeted comprehensive approach that we are looking to expand and make sure that that tree planting work gets done on a comprehensive level within nine years' time. I do believe because it has to do with canopy and because this is very important to us, looking at that 30 percent number, that this is in close partnership also with our sister agency at MOCEJ so I'm going to look to our Climate Officer to see if she'd like to add anything to that.

Thank you, Commissioner, and thank you, Council Member, for that question. As I think I mentioned in an earlier response, part of our work with the Urban Forest Plan is also to make sure that we have good systems of accountability in place to make sure that we are doing exactly that, tracking our progress and making sure we understand the changes in our tree canopy over time. So, what that will look like is every five years, we will be doing a LIDAR survey that basically covers all of the areas citywide to do a very detailed stock take of all of the different trees, the species, the canopy size, and so the data that we looked at to inform our plan analysis was for the five-year period of 2017 to 2021. And now going forward, we'll have that five-year analysis as a consistent way to benchmark our progress. So, we definitely want to make sure that we're using data-driven approaches and to reach those equity goals that the Commissioner mentioned.

Thank you. And lastly, regarding the storm and risk mitigations, in light of the increased frequency of extreme weather

events, how is DPR's attempting its tree care programs to ensure that trees are resilient against storms, hurricanes, and blizzards? For instance, how does DPR prepare for the impact of snowstorms like the one that we just experienced this past February, 2026, which resulted in significant tree damage? And can you share the details about DPR's emergency response system in the aftermath of severe weather, including response times and the current readiness for tree damage restoration?

Of course. So, I will just say that while it would seem that we could do a lot to prepare for storms like this, like we just experienced, ultimately trees are susceptible to any type of weather and the tree issues that come up can come up for a number of different reasons. The only way that we, the best, I guess, offense that we have in these situations is through regular pruning. That is the industry standard, but even so, you could see a newly planted tree that ultimately falls and fails due to extreme weather. You can see a larger tree, ultimately, as you probably saw in the news, fail because of extreme weather. That doesn't really make a difference. What we see, though, is that with

regular pruning, that can be the best offense that we provide, and that's why we are committed to pruning on a seven-year cycle. That's industry standard in order to make sure that those trees are regularly pruned and able to withstand this type of extreme weather. In addition to that, we do have a whole winter weather response plan that is formed every year that we follow through on that I referenced earlier in terms of how we plow, how we clear snow. We also have the Downed Trees Task Force, which gets activated when we see blizzard conditions coming up, and we are in extremely close communication with our partners at NYCEM and other sister agencies as the storm kind of is gearing up so that we're ready to go once the storm ends and we can get to work.
Thank you. We're going to move over to Council Member Marte.

Thank you, Chair. First of all, I want to say congratulations, Commissioner. I'm so excited to have you in this new role. As Borough Commissioner, you were literally the best. You showed up almost in every single part of my District, and so I'm sure a lot of the garden

activists and park activists are excited about your tenure as Commissioner, so congratulations. I've been looking at the map during this meeting, and I want to say what you guys have said is actually correct. You've been focusing mostly on environmental justice communities as part of the initial phases of your plan, so it's great to see large parts of the Lower East Side and Chinatown in my District as part of that first phase. My question is in regards to a lot of the resiliency projects that we have downtown. There are commitments made for a fund to help plant trees to mitigate some of the trees that were lost during construction and demolition of East River Park. Would this phasing approach stop the planting of trees in that area that were supposed to be committed to by Parks on a timely basis, or how do you juggle previous commitments of planting compared to this new holistic phasing strategy that you have?

Thank you so much for the question, and thank you for your ongoing partnership. Let me just say from the top that no one takes more seriously the loss of healthy trees than

our agency. Before any plan goes before a community board and gets presented to you or any other public body, we closely pressure test and truly debate behind closed doors the merits and what is lost when we lose one of our healthy trees. As I mentioned before, we have a serious mandate to get to 30 percent canopy, and we know that planting new trees is wonderful and a part of that plan, but taking care of the trees that we have, those adult mature trees that provide so much canopy, that's the only way that we're going to get to 30 percent, and so we take the loss of healthy trees extremely seriously. Now, we are doing our comprehensive planting plan, but I believe that when it comes to other projects, like what you're maybe referencing with our Eastside Coastal Resiliency Project or other things like that, those, I believe, are on separate timeframes, and so separate projects. This is what we're doing kind of through our maybe bread and butter of Forestry Planting Team, but on top of that, when it comes to these other commitments made, we have those, I believe, on a separate timeframe. I'm going to look to Matt Drury from our team to give us a little bit more detail there, but ultimately, that loss of trees

is something, and I hope your constituents know this personally, but it bears repeating. It's something that we take very seriously.

Yeah. Just if I can help clarify, the Neighborhood Tree Planting Program that the Commissioner has described, and as you mentioned with the plan timeframe, that is focused on street tree planting, and so any effort for a park improvement project, capital project, as the Commissioner mentioned, we look for every opportunity to minimize any impacts on trees that are within our parks, but if and when it is necessary, obviously replacement well over and above what's removed is certainly always the plan, and additionally, through any capital renovation project, we're always looking for opportunities. It is actually built into our landscape design process that our capital division team leads to look for planting opportunities within that park or playground or sitting area or what have you, so the short answer is I think we can reach out to our partners at DDC and others to get you an update in terms of that timeline and those efforts, because that is sort of separated apart from the Neighborhood Tree Planting Program.
I think specifically there was a commitment to plant trees throughout the Lower East Side because of the park being under construction.
Yes. And to address that specifically, that commitment is being worked into our Neighborhood Tree Planting Plan. It's not being replaced by our Neighborhood Tree Planting Plan.

Okay. I would just love to follow up on timing, because there are some areas around East River Park that look like they're in phase three, and so that means they won't get the tree until much, much later than expected.
Absolutely. We can follow up with you on timing.
All right. Thank you so much.
We're going to jump to Council Member Brewer.

Thank you very much. I want to congratulate the climate, whatever the hell your title is, whatever, Chief Climate Officer and the Commissioner of Parks. They're both fabulous.

Okay. So, I have four questions. I'll go them, and then you can decide how to answer. The first is just how many trees, I think you said there were 1,800 service requests that came down in the recent storm, and two of them on my block, so I'm very familiar with this issue. So, I have two questions. How many weather-related in 2-5, sort of similar so I can get a sense of how many trees were either down or there were complaints? And then second, just in terms of those that did get the service requests, in some cases, I guess it's a huge branch. That's what happened in my area. And then the whole street is full of branches and pain-in-the-neck neighbors who call 3-1-1 every five minutes. So, is that Sanitation or you who cleans up? That's question number one, and then including the data. Number two, just like you, I am a tree hugger. So, I want to say, and that's why I have so many people here today, that we have tree care clinics, even just put it in our recent newsletter, constantly. So, we do feel very strongly about tree care, because you can't have a new tree and not have somebody caring for it. And I think you sort of said that, but I would say that very, very loudly.

Number three, we have a letter that was sent before your term, August 25, 23 Council Members signed. I do not like this program that you like so much. And I'll tell you why. I have four years, 38 of us have four years. Nine years and four years do not compute in terms of getting our trees planted. So, the political calendar does not fit with the tree calendar. So, that has to fit better. So, my question is, how we can do a parallel process? Because I understand that some areas have not had trees and you've got floods and blah, blah, blah so we need a parallel process, I think, to work on. So, I want to know what that would cost, because I mean, literally, if you want to pick the most popular topic in the City of New York, it is street trees. So, the question is how much it would cost. Now I have some numbers for an area, my area, for two years, 79 street trees, plus taking out the stumps cost 250,000. So, take 250,000, 79, and multiply that times all the trees needed. What is the number that you actually need to do a parallel or faster process than this nine-year thing that everybody I know hates, just so you know.

And then the issue of Local Law 84 of 2013 that we put into, and this is climate related, we put into that planning process, and I think you're saying that, that trees are part of air and water and all the issues regarding climate, and I think that's correct, I just want to double check. Those are my four questions.

Great. Okay. So, I'm going to try to do all of them, save for one, and then pass that one to MOCEJ. I think that last one is all for her. OkAy. So, let me just, the easy one at first is that the 1,800 number that we referenced in the recent storm of 3-1-1 complaints, all of those were storm related-complaints.
For this recent storm.
Just this recent storm.
Okay.

Now there were some duplicates, so ultimately that resulted in 1,200 inspections that needed to come in place, so there were some duplicates, and from those 1,200, we had 47

downed trees in streets, so those were our top priority, get those streets clear, make sure that emergency vehicles can go through, and then I believe nine were large trees or limbs that fell onto property, and those were our next priority.
But those 47 will not be replaced unless it's within the, you know, whatever, location.
Yeah. We would be looking to plant those within our Tree Planting Plan.
Okay. That's the thing we don't like. Okay. Go ahead.
I'll go to that one next. And of course, within our season, so we wouldn't be planting anything right now.
No. I understand. I got that part.
So, I mean, I definitely hear you on the nine-year timeframe. I am very proud of us for looking at the larger picture here --
I agree.

-- but I understand the frustrations around nine years being

too long of a time, so what I can tell you is that we are constantly looking at ways that we can speed this up. We are constantly trying to hold ourselves accountable for not being stuck in a system that just is because it's always been this way, and instead are trying to --
I understand.
-- look creatively at this.
I call it the parallel process.
I will certainly look into --
Okay.

-- your suggestion, but I will point out that it's not just about planting new trees, so that 250,000-dollar number, what I'd point out is that what we're doing is it's planting trees plus. It's expanding those tree beds, it's taking out those stumps.
The 250 included all that. The 250,000 included all of that, just so you know. Every bit of it.

And then one more and then I'll pass over to my colleagues at MOCEJ but thank you for being a tree hugger, thank you for being a tree lover. What I'd say is that you can actually still get involved in addition to hosting stewardship events which I know that you do. We are still in the process of doing our decennial tree count, so if your office would like to host a tree count event where we're counting trees, categorizing trees.
I only want to count them if they're going to be planted. Otherwise, I do not want to plant to count them.
We are certainly planting, but we'd love to have your participation and then I'll pass over to, oh.

And then sorry, just quickly, you mentioned about tree debris and I'll just clarify that. That is a shared responsibility between DSNY and Parks following serious storms. Tree, just along with leaf and yard waste can be left out as part of the City's Organic Recycling Program for sure. Obviously, sometimes there are larger limbs.
These are huge limbs, huge limbs, so that would be.
So, those would be 3-1-1 requests that are tracked and then I guess, you know.
Somebody will figure it out.
I know you love your parallel paths. You know that's something that both DSNY and Parks sort of, you know, we coordinate for sure but those are sort of jointly responsible I would say.
Okay.

And thank you, Council Member, for your question about trees and the role that they play in addressing our climate crisis. So in 2025, thank you for Council Member support in passing Local Law 149 which, you know, amended the Comprehensive Climate Stability Plans. That did make sure that trees are part of that mandate. As many of us have mentioned here today, trees are a really critical aspect of how we address climate change. They provide heat resiliency and necessary shade during heat waves, they capture storm water, they clean our air, they're better for our

mental health, they're better for quality of life, and so we are really excited to make sure that trees are an integral part of our green infrastructure.
The only thing I need, not now, is the total cost it would cost to do every single vacant tree pit plus stump removal. What is the total cost? Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. I want to acknowledge Council Members Lee and Restler who we've been joined by. And now I want to go over to Brooklyn, Council Member Narcisse.

Thank you. Like Gale, I love trees and it's a necessity for me. So first, congratulations. And with all that, I want to say, because what are the primary reasons for the delay of pruning? I heard both of my Colleagues talking about it. Is this staffing shortage, contractor capacity, or budget constraint or something else? Because it's a problem in my community.

Sure. Thank you so much for your question. I would just say that one,

there is such a thing as too much pruning as my husband always reminds me because I tend to pick too many things up of our home plants, but it also is something that we've already been committed to pruning at one every seven years, and so I would suggest that that actually is still meeting the industry standard. We typically don't prune any more than that just because then we start to risk the health of the tree. So every seven years, you should see your trees pruned. That is what we're meeting, the mark that we're meeting and we're doing so primarily through enlisting contractors to help us do that kind of neighborhood block pruning. Anything that's specialty, anything that's a little bit more of an emergency situation, anything that's requiring additional assistance, that's where you see our in-house team go in there because we have that expertise, we have that skillset that we're able to address some of those more specific conditions. But your typical pruning, your constituents should see us in their neighborhoods every seven years, which is industry standard.
Some of them goes beyond the seven years, but anyway.

If you'd like, I can add just a little bit to that, which is that through our tree risk management approach, those requests that we receive for pruning in between that seven-year cycle, those requests are evaluated, they're ranked according to priority category A through D, with A being the most urgent, and those work orders and priority categories, A through B, we respond to within seven or 28 days, respectively, 99 percent of the time. So, the most urgent conditions are addressed very quickly. We understand that there are other conditions that are --
There are other conditions.
-- there are real conditions that we don't get to as quick as some people would like.

So, my office receive a lot of calls on those trees because you know, as we have so many trees, but I would have another question too. After Sandy, we lost so many trees, but I haven't seen that replacement yet. We're talking about since 2012. So, I want to know where we are. That's a private conversation because we need

trees in our community. I have some of the trees, right? The resident complained about them. There's a hazard. We can tell they're hazard, right? But yet when the Park come to inspect them, they always find them in fair conditions. And when we have a storm, sure enough, they will fall down and damage, which is we call it penny wise, dollar foolish. We should push to fix that so we don't spend more money at the end. Can you explain how Parks define fair condition? What metrics that you use? What's the process? Because you say fair condition, but my eyes telling me this is crazy.

Absolutely. So, I want to address the first part of your question and then I'll look to our Assistant Commissioner to talk through the details. And what I'll say is that I'm so grateful for your question because I want you to be able to articulate to your constituents what rating system is used and the industry standards that we're using so that everybody can understand the same metrics that we're using. It's really important to me. And when it comes to planting, we absolutely are happy to make sure that we get you a schedule of when your plantings are coming into your District. We want

your constituents to be excited about this. We want them to see that we're delivering for you and this neighborhood so we're happy to come back to you with that. But I'm going to look to Ben to give you very specifics around what fair means.
And when a tree come out or fail, whatever the reason, when do we get another one, the replacement? Do we replace them automatically or something that -- yeah, go ahead.

Sure. So, I'll respond to that last question first and then go back to your question about fair condition. So, as the Commissioner described our Neighborhood Tree Planting Program, that is the primary driver of the timeframe for when we are planting trees. So, it will depend on exactly where that tree is on what block it is in terms of when it would be replaced. There's not a specific time based on when a tree is removed or fails. In terms of what we mean when we say a tree is in fair condition and how that affects what is going to happen, that's just a very qualitative description. If somebody calls about a tree and

they're concerned about the safety from that tree, we look at the entire tree. We look at whether it has any dead branches, any decay, poor structural issues, and each of those potential issues is given a full risk assessment that looks at the likelihood of that tree or part failing, the likelihood of it falling onto people or property and the consequences should that occur, and that gives a risk rating for that condition. Now, if the tree's in fair condition and we see a branch that has a risk rating that determines work should be done, we're going to prune that tree. We'll schedule it for pruning. If the tree's in poor condition and we see similar types of problems, we may consider removing the tree instead. So, I realize it's a little bit confusing, this kind of fair, good, poor condition because that's not determining whether or not work is performed and maybe driving the type of work we decide to do so I think we could be a little bit more clear about that in our communications.

And so my time is coming to an end. What are the eligibility requirements for the Trees and Sidewalk Program? And are there plans

to expand it so homeowners don't have to pay out of pocket when the roots cause sidewalk damage? And especially, I have a lot of seniors in my community that are living on tight budgets. So, what can we do?

Sure. So, yeah. We understand this is something we hear about with frequency, right? So, the Tax Class One properties in New York City are eligible for the Trees and Sidewalks Program if the roots of a tree under Parks jurisdiction have damaged the sidewalk. So, those are one- to three-family residential properties. When we receive a request for that program, we perform a rating. We send an inspector who performs a rating that's based on the size and number and health of the existing trees, the extent and severity of a tripping hazard that may be present, and generators of foot traffic in the area, subway stations, churches, schools, et cetera, and that all rolls up into a rating that may be up to 100, anywhere from one to 100. It's a very popular program and the resources are limited. So, with the current funding levels that we have, we're able to repair sites that are rated 90 and higher across the city and, depending on the number of sites in a given

area, some sites that are rated lower. And we acknowledge that that leaves some legitimate issues unaddressed. It's important to note, however, that property owners are not liable in these cases for tripping hazards resulting from the roots of City trees, and the City is not holding those property owners financially responsible. You know, should they receive a violation for other defects on their sidewalk from DOT, any portion damaged by the tree, DOT would not assess the property owner for, and they would not issue a violation only for root damage from City trees, and our program is free. So, while this is a real concern --
It is.
-- property owners are not liable for these conditions and nobody is forcing them to be financially responsible.
Thank you. And Madam Commissioner, again, congratulations. And I hope we can improve in the construction when it comes to Parks. That's another story so we'll talk. Thank you.
All right. Really briefly, while we still have quorum, I'm going to jump to Southern Brooklyn to Council Member Santosuosso, who's on Zoom.

Good morning. Can everybody hear me? Okay. First of all, thank you so much, Chair, and thank you to the Commissioners for being here today. Congratulations as well. I want to just start by saying, I have the experience of being someone who has dealt with forestry issues from the perspective of working in a Council Member's office and being a Council Member, but also someone who worked at the Law Department and was a tort division attorney where I handled some of the cases that result from things like fallen branches or when suits are brought against the City and homeowners for sidewalks that are lifted by tree roots so, I bring that dual perspective. So, I'm going to be mostly talking about tree maintenance in my questions and a little bit about sort of the costs at every step. My understanding based on data that was given to me by New Yorkers for Parks, and maybe you said this in your testimony, I'm sorry if I

missed it, but is that NYC Parks has a backlog of more than 20,000 uninspected tree conditions and 35,000 unaddressed work orders. And while a new tree costs about 3,600 dollars to plant and takes years to mature, so maintaining our existing street trees is particularly important and also cost-effective. And so, I want to just first ask, I know you said that there are 60 foresters in the Department. How many inspectors are there or is that captured within the foresters number?

Sure. Hi, Council Member. Thank you so much. I hope you can hear me okay. Thank you so much for your question. I'll just give some confirmation of some of the numbers that you referenced and then I'll look to our Assistant Commissioner who oversees our Forestry Unit to give you confirmation on the exact staffing numbers. So yes, it is true. I've referenced it earlier too that we do have a backlog of tree risk orders here. That backlog is around 34,000 tree risk work orders. We also have 17,000 uninspected service requests that includes the kind of more of the Trees and Sidewalks Program that you were referencing. I

will just say that while this backlog does exist, the requests that are coming in are hopefully not all in that extreme high-risk category. They're not the sort of situations where we would see them as an emergency situations. All of these requests that are coming in that have not been fully inspected have been screened at a high level to make sure that we are still responding to those very serious immediate emergency situations. Where we see this backlog exists is in those categories C and D levels. So, in the rating system that we use is those kind of more moderate level risks that are still very serious, but not those in extreme emergencies. Now, I want to get to your other question around staffing. So, I'm going to pass it over to our Assistant Commissioner to tell you the exact staffing levels.

Thank you, Council Member, for those questions. And just quickly on the numbers, one more thing. You referenced the cost of tree planting. In Fiscal Year 2022, that the average cost for tree planting was 3,550 dollars. That's actually come down quite a bit. It is currently 2,900 dollars citywide. So that's an

18 percent reduction. Actually adjusted for inflation, that's 37 percent of a reduction. To your question about staffing, the 60 foresters we have, those are inspectors. However, we do have some people in other titles that serve in an inspection role as well. Some of our climber pruners perform inspections and supervisors and handful of other people, but the bulk of our inspections are performed by the 60 foresters.

Understood. And so, and I just want to say, Commissioner, and I totally appreciate that we prioritize complaints as they come in for the most urgent, but I think we get a lot on our end of C and D category complaints that feel urgent to the constituent, and then sometimes when we have an intense storm result in the constituent calling our office and saying, well, I tried to put this limb that was hanging on Parks radar, but they said it wasn't going to be inspected until 2027.
